```{r setup}
# load packages
library(tidyverse)   # for data wrangling and visualization
library(ggformula)   # for plotting using formulas
library(broom)       # for formatting model output
library(knitr)       # for pretty tables
library(kableExtra)  # also for pretty tables
library(coursekata)
library(plotly)      # for the 3D pictures

# DC bikeshare: used for the prediction section and the quantitative interactions
bikeshare <- read_csv(here::here("data/dcbikeshare.csv")) |>
  mutate(
    season = case_when(
      season == 1 ~ "winter",
      season == 2 ~ "spring",
      season == 3 ~ "summer",
      season == 4 ~ "fall"),
    season = factor(season, levels = c("winter", "spring", "summer", "fall"))
  )

# Framingham Heart Study: the data for the three interaction cases
fram <- read_csv(here::here("data/framingham.csv")) |>
  drop_na(sysBP) |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(if_else(male == 1, "Male", "Female"), levels = c("Female", "Male")),
    diabetes_status = factor(if_else(diabetes == 1, "Diabetic", "Not diabetic"),
                             levels = c("Not diabetic", "Diabetic"))
  )

# group means and plot helpers for the diabetes x sex slides
cell_means <- fram |>
  group_by(sex, diabetes_status) |>
  summarize(mean_bp = mean(sysBP), n = n(), .groups = "drop")

sex_colors <- c(Female = "#E4572E", Male = "#1F77B4")

# one line per sex through `line_means` (one value per row of cell_means), with the four
# actual group means as diamonds. Optionally show the jittered data, the labeled means, and
# an x at each model prediction (the end points of the lines).
bp_plot <- function(line_means, show_data = TRUE, show_labels = TRUE, show_predictions = FALSE) {
  dodge <- position_dodge(width = 0.6)
  p <- gf_point(sysBP ~ diabetes_status, data = fram, color = ~ sex,
                alpha = if (show_data) 0.25 else 0, size = 1.5,
                position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.15, jitter.height = 0, dodge.width = 0.6)) |>
    gf_line(line_means ~ diabetes_status, data = mutate(cell_means, line_means = line_means),
            color = ~ sex, group = ~ sex, linewidth = 1.2, position = dodge) |>
    gf_point(mean_bp ~ diabetes_status, data = cell_means, fill = ~ sex, group = ~ sex,
             color = "black", size = 5, shape = 23, stroke = 1.5, position = dodge)
  if (show_predictions) {
    p <- p |>
      gf_point(line_means ~ diabetes_status, data = mutate(cell_means, line_means = line_means),
               group = ~ sex, color = "black", shape = 4, size = 5, stroke = 2, position = dodge)
  }
  if (show_labels) {
    p <- p |>
      gf_label(mean_bp ~ x_pos,
               data = mutate(cell_means, x_pos = as.numeric(diabetes_status) + if_else(sex == "Female", -0.15, 0.15)),
               label = ~ round(mean_bp, 1), color = ~ sex, fill = "white",
               vjust = -0.7, size = 6, fontface = "bold", show.legend = FALSE)
  }
  p |>
    gf_refine(scale_color_manual(values = sex_colors),
              scale_fill_manual(values = sex_colors),
              guides(fill = "none")) |>
    gf_labs(x = "Diabetes status", y = "Systolic BP (mm Hg)", color = "Sex")
}

# the same picture with each coefficient of the interaction model marked on it.
# `b` holds the coefficients named b0, b1, b2, b3 (see the model equation slide).
beta_plot <- function(b) {
  y0 <- b[["b0"]]                 # Female, Not diabetic
  y1 <- y0 + b[["b1"]]            # Female, Diabetic
  ym0 <- y0 + b[["b2"]]           # Male, Not diabetic
  ypar <- y1 + b[["b2"]]          # Male, Diabetic if the lines were parallel
  ym1 <- ypar + b[["b3"]]         # Male, Diabetic (actual)
  fmt <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x)
  bp_plot(cell_means$mean_bp, show_data = FALSE, show_labels = FALSE) +
    annotate("segment", x = 0.85, xend = 1.85, y = y0, yend = y0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey30") +
    annotate("segment", x = 1.85, xend = 1.85, y = y0, yend = y1, linewidth = 1.6, colour = "grey20") +
    annotate("segment", x = 1.15, xend = 1.15, y = y0, yend = ym0, linewidth = 1.6, colour = "grey20") +
    annotate("segment", x = 1.15, xend = 2.15, y = ym0, yend = ypar, linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 1,
             colour = sex_colors[["Male"]]) +
    annotate("segment", x = 2.15, xend = 2.15, y = ypar, yend = ym1, linewidth = 1.6, colour = "grey20") +
    annotate("label", x = 0.78, y = y0, label = paste0("hat(beta)[0]==", fmt(y0)),
             parse = TRUE, size = 5, fill = "white", hjust = 1) +
    annotate("label", x = 1.22, y = ym0 - 2.5, label = paste0("hat(beta)[2]==", fmt(b[["b2"]])),
             parse = TRUE, size = 5, fill = "white", hjust = 0) +
    annotate("label", x = 1.8, y = (y0 + y1) / 2 + 3, label = paste0("hat(beta)[1]==", fmt(b[["b1"]])),
             parse = TRUE, size = 5, fill = "white", hjust = 1) +
    annotate("label", x = 2.22, y = (ypar + ym1) / 2, label = paste0("hat(beta)[3]==", fmt(b[["b3"]])),
             parse = TRUE, size = 5, fill = "white", hjust = 0) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(122, 158), xlim = c(0.3, 2.7))
}

# the additive model from last time
mlr_fit <- lm(count ~ temp_orig + season, data = bikeshare)

# 3D helper for the two-quantitative case (same plotly pattern as the old categorical-predictors deck).
# surface_z(): predictions on a grid, one row per y value and one column per x value.
surface_z <- function(fit, xs, ys, xname, yname) {
  grid <- expand.grid(xs, ys)
  names(grid) <- c(xname, yname)
  matrix(predict(fit, grid), nrow = length(ys), byrow = TRUE)
}

# surface_plot(): 3D scatterplot of the data with a model surface on top
surface_plot <- function(data, x, y, z, zmat, xs, ys, labels, point_color = "red") {
  plot_ly(data, x = data[[x]], y = data[[y]], z = data[[z]],
          color = I(point_color), opacity = 1,
          type = "scatter3d", mode = "markers", size = 1) |>
    add_surface(x = xs, y = ys, z = zmat, opacity = 0.8,
                inherit = FALSE, showscale = FALSE) |>
    layout(scene = list(xaxis = list(title = labels[1]),
                        yaxis = list(title = labels[2]),
                        zaxis = list(title = labels[3])),
           autosize = TRUE,
           margin = list(l = 0, r = 0, t = 0, b = 0)) |>
    config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
}
```

# Review: AE 17

## Where we are {.smaller}

Last time we fit our first multiple regression on the coffee truck: `Sales` from `Temperature` **and** a categorical variable.

```{r}
#| echo: false
ae_fit <- lm(Sales ~ Temperature + Location, data = coffee)
ae_fit |> tidy() |> kable(digits = 2)
```

::: question
Interpret the `Temperature` coefficient and the `LocationZoo` coefficient. What does the fitted picture look like?
:::

. . .

- `Temperature`: holding `Location` constant, each extra °F is associated with about `r abs(round(coef(ae_fit)[2], 2))` fewer cups.
- `LocationZoo`: holding `Temperature` constant, the Zoo sells about `r abs(round(coef(ae_fit)[5]))` fewer cups than the Business District.
- The fitted picture is **parallel lines**: one slope, one intercept per location.

- **Do not extrapolate!** With several predictors you can extrapolate in many directions at once, even when each predictor is individually in range.


```{r}

library(patchwork) 
p1 <- bikeshare |> 
  gf_histogram(~temp_orig)
p2 <- bikeshare |>

p1 + p2
```

Would you trust a prediction for a 30°C winter day?

## Cautions {.smaller}

- **Do not extrapolate!** With several predictors you can extrapolate in many directions at once, even when each predictor is individually in range.


```{r}
#| echo: false
p1 <- bikeshare |> 
  gf_histogram(~temp_orig)
p2 <- bikeshare |> 
  gf_boxplot(temp_orig ~ season)

p1 + p2
```

Would you trust a prediction for a 30°C winter day?

## From parallel lines to interactions {.smaller}

Every model so far has been **additive**: the effect of one variable is the same at every value of the other. In a plot, that means **parallel lines**.

::: question
Is it believable that an extra degree adds the same number of rentals in winter as in summer? That diabetes raises blood pressure by the same amount for men and for women?
:::

. . .

Today:

1. Conceptualizing models with two predictors.
2. Three cases, one picture each: **two categorical** (group means), **one of each** (lines), **two quantitative** (a surface).
3. **AE 18**.

# Interaction Terms

## Interaction means multiplication {.smaller}

With two explanatory variables $X_1$ and $X_2$, our model is purely additive.

$$
\text{additive:}\quad \mu_Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2
$$

. . .

Adding an interaction term, multiplies two variables, treating the product like a new variable:

. . .

$$
\text{with interaction:}\quad \mu_Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \beta_3 X_1 X_2
$$

. . .

Intuition: The impact of $X_1$ on $Y$, depends on the value of $X_2$ (and vice versa)

# Case 1: Two categorical variables

## The data {.smaller}

The Framingham Heart Study, as in Lectures 15 and 16. Our response is systolic blood pressure (`sysBP`, mm Hg).

```{r}
#| echo: false
fram |>
  select(sysBP, sex, diabetes_status, age, BMI, totChol) |>
  glimpse()
```

- `sex`: Female or Male.
- `diabetes_status`: Not diabetic or Diabetic.
- `age` (years), `BMI`, and `totChol` (total cholesterol, mg/dL): we will use these later.

## Modeling blood pressure from sex and diabetes {.smaller}

Let's start with what we know: an **additive** model with both predictors.

```{r}
add_fit <- lm(sysBP ~ diabetes_status + sex, data = fram)
add_fit |> tidy() |> kable(digits = 2)
```

This model says the effect of diabetes is **the same** for men and for women (and the male vs. female difference is the same whether or not someone has diabetes).

## What this model actually is {.smaller}

An additive model is just the **grand mean** plus one **effect** for each variable. Each effect is how far a group's **marginal mean** sits from the grand mean:

$$
\widehat{\text{sysBP}} = \underbrace{\bar y_{\text{ND}\cdot} + \bar y_{\cdot\text{F}} - \bar y}_{\hat\beta_0} + \underbrace{(\bar y_{\text{D}\cdot} - \bar y_{\text{ND}\cdot})}_{\hat\beta_1}\,\text{Diabetic} + \underbrace{(\bar y_{\cdot\text{M}} - \bar y_{\cdot\text{F}})}_{\hat\beta_2}\,\text{Male}
$$

- $\bar{y}$: mean `sysBP` of everyone
- $\bar y_{\text{ND}\cdot}$ and $\bar y_{\text{D}\cdot}$: mean of `sysBP` for just people without or with diabetes
- $\bar y_{\cdot M}$ and $\bar y_{\cdot M}$: mean of `sysBP` for just males or just females

## Visualizing the Model {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| out.width: "65%"
bp_plot(predict(add_fit, cell_means), show_predictions = TRUE)
```

- Lines and **x** marks show the model's predicted mean for each group
- Diamonds show the **actual** mean of each group.

::: question 
Does it look like the impact of diabetes depends on sex? If so, does our model capture that?
:::

## What do the data say? {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
cell_means |>
  select(-n) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = diabetes_status, values_from = mean_bp) |>
  kable(digits = 1)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| out.width: "65%"
bp_plot(cell_means$mean_bp)
```

::: question
Does diabetes change blood pressure by the same amount for men and for women?
:::

##  It doesn't look like it! {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
mu <- function(s, d) cell_means$mean_bp[cell_means$sex == s & cell_means$diabetes_status == d]
```

- **Women:** diabetes goes with a blood pressure about `r round(mu("Female", "Diabetic") - mu("Female", "Not diabetic"))` mm Hg higher.
- **Men:** diabetes goes with a blood pressure about `r round(mu("Male", "Diabetic") - mu("Male", "Not diabetic"))` mm Hg higher.

. . .

When the effect of `diabetes_status` **depends on** `sex`, we say there is an **interaction** between `diabetes_status` and `sex`.


# The interaction model

## Building the interaction term by hand {.smaller}

An interaction term is just a **new column**: the product of the two 0/1 (dummy) variables.

```{r}
#| echo: false
fram_int <- fram |>
  mutate(
    diabetic = if_else(diabetes_status == "Diabetic", 1, 0),
    is_male = if_else(sex == "Male", 1, 0),
    diabetic_male = diabetic * is_male
  )

fram_int |>
  count(diabetes_status, sex, diabetic, is_male, diabetic_male) |>
  kable()
```

. . .

The product `diabetic_male` is 1 **only** for men with diabetes, and 0 for everyone else.

. . .

The model with an interaction term is:

$$
\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \beta_3 X_1\times X_2 + \epsilon
$$

. . .

Always include the single order terms (i.e. $\beta_1 X_1$ and $\beta_2 X_2$)

## Adding an interaction {.smaller}

To let the diabetes effect differ by sex, we add the **product** of the indicator variables:

```{r}
int_fit <- lm(sysBP ~ diabetes_status * sex, data = fram)
int_fit |> tidy() |> kable(digits = 2)
```

`diabetes_status * sex` will automatically add the single order terms

## The model equation {.smaller}

With the reference levels Not diabetic and Female:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\text{sysBP}} = &\hat\beta_0 \\
&+ \hat\beta_1 \,\text{Diabetic} + \hat\beta_2 \,\text{Male} \\
&\underbrace{+ \hat\beta_3 \,(\text{Diabetic} \times \text{Male})}_{\text{interaction term}}
\end{aligned}
$$

```{r}
#| echo: false
b <- coef(int_fit)
names(b) <- c("b0", "b1", "b2", "b3")

# number with an explicit sign, for building the equation
sgn <- function(x) sprintf("%+.1f", x)
```

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\text{sysBP}} = &`r round(b["b0"], 1)` \\
&`r sgn(b["b1"])` \,\text{Diabetic} `r sgn(b["b2"])` \,\text{Male} \\
&\underbrace{`r sgn(b["b3"])` \,(\text{Diabetic} \times \text{Male})}_{\text{interaction term}}
\end{aligned}
$$

```{r}
#| echo: false
fram |> group_by(sex, diabetes) |> summarize(avg_sysBP = mean(sysBP)) |> kable()
``` 

::: question
On the board, show that the model is just predicting the mean of each group.
:::

## Recovering the cell means {.smaller}

Each of the four means is the sum of the terms that are "on":

```{r}
#| echo: false
tibble(
  Combination = c("Female, Not diabetic", "Female, Diabetic", "Male, Not diabetic", "Male, Diabetic"),
  `Terms on` = c("b0", "b0 + b1", "b0 + b2", "b0 + b1 + b2 + b3"),
  `Model value` = c(b["b0"], b["b0"] + b["b1"], b["b0"] + b["b2"],
                    b["b0"] + b["b1"] + b["b2"] + b["b3"])
) |>
  kable(digits = 1)
```

. . .

The interaction model reproduces all four means exactly. It has one parameter per cell.

## Interpreting the interaction term {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}
- $\hat\beta_0$: the mean for the reference group, **non-diabetic women**.
- $\hat\beta_1$ (`diabetes_statusDiabetic`): the diabetes effect **for women** (the reference sex). It is *not* the overall diabetes effect anymore.
- $\hat\beta_2$ (`sexMale`): Male minus Female **among non-diabetic participants** (the reference diabetes status).
- $\hat\beta_3$ (`diabetes_statusDiabetic:sexMale`): how much **bigger** (or smaller) the diabetes effect is for men than for women. The **gap** between the dotted line (men if the lines were parallel) and the actual men's mean.
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| out.width: "100%"
beta_plot(b)
```
:::

::::

# Case 2: Categorical-Quantitative Interaction

## Is the age slope the same for men and women? {.smaller}

Now let's predict `sysBP` from `age` and `sex`. An additive model gives one slope for age and a different intercept for each sex.

```{r}
#| echo: false
age_add <- lm(sysBP ~ age + sex, data = fram)
age_int <- lm(sysBP ~ age * sex, data = fram)

augment(age_add) |>
  gf_point(sysBP ~ age, color = ~ sex, alpha = 0.15, size = 0.5) |>
  gf_line(.fitted ~ age, color = ~ sex, linewidth = .5) |>
  gf_refine(scale_color_manual(values = sex_colors)) |>
  gf_labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Systolic BP (mm Hg)", color = "Sex", title = "Additive: parallel lines")
```

::: question
Do we believe that men and women age in the same way?
:::

## Letting the slope depend on sex {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
augment(age_int) |>
  gf_point(sysBP ~ age, color = ~ sex, alpha = 0.15, size-0.5) |>
  gf_line(.fitted ~ age, color = ~ sex, linewidth = .5) |>
  gf_refine(scale_color_manual(values = sex_colors)) |>
  gf_labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Systolic BP (mm Hg)", color = "Sex", title = "Interaction: a separate slope for each sex")
```

::: question
Which group's blood pressure rises faster with age? At what age do the lines nearly meet?
:::

## Slopes by sex {.smaller}

```{r}
age_int <- lm(sysBP ~ age * sex, data = fram)
age_int |> tidy() |> kable(digits = 2)
```

- Women (the reference level): slope $\hat\beta_1$ = `r round(coef(age_int)["age"], 2)` mm Hg per year.
- Men: slope $\hat\beta_1 + \hat\beta_3$ = `r round(coef(age_int)["age"] + coef(age_int)["age:sexMale"], 2)` mm Hg per year.

::: question
- What does the negative interaction coefficient say about how blood pressure changes with age for men compared with women?
- One the board, write out the two lines nested in this model: the male line and the female line
:::

# Case 3: Two quantitative

## Age and BMI {.smaller}

Finally, two quantitative predictors. Let's predict total cholesterol (`totChol`, mg/dL) from:

- $X_1$ = `age` (years), $X_2$ = `BMI`.

We'll compare two models:

::::{.columns}
:::{.column}
#### Additive Model (no interaction)

$$
\widehat{\text{totChol}} = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \,\text{age} + \hat\beta_2 \,\text{BMI}
$$

```{r}
lm(totChol ~ age + BMI, data = fram) |> tidy() |> kable()
```
:::
:::{.column}
#### Interaction Model

$$
\widehat{\text{totChol}} = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \,\text{age} + \hat\beta_2 \,\text{BMI} + \hat\beta_3 \,(\text{age} \times \text{BMI})
$$

```{r}
lm(totChol ~ age * BMI, data = fram) |> tidy() |> kable()
```
:::
::::

::: question
Break into four groups. Each group write the equations for a line on the board (one from each model):

- Group 1: Fix BMI = 20
- Group 2: Fix BMI = 30
- Group 3: Fix age = 35
- Group 4: Fix age = 70
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
quant_add <- lm(totChol ~ age + BMI, data = fram)
quant_int <- lm(totChol ~ age * BMI, data = fram)

# the 3D pictures show 600 randomly chosen participants (plotting all 4,000+ is slow)
set.seed(2026)
fram_pts <- fram |>
  drop_na(totChol, BMI) |>
  filter(totChol < 400, BMI < 45) |>
  slice_sample(n = 600)

quant_xs <- seq(min(fram$age), max(fram$age), length.out = 30)
quant_ys <- seq(17, 40, length.out = 30)
quant_labels <- c("Age (years)", "BMI", "Total cholesterol")
```

## Additive: a flat plane {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| dpi: 96
surface_plot(fram_pts, "age", "BMI", "totChol",
             surface_z(quant_add, quant_xs, quant_ys, "age", "BMI"),
             quant_xs, quant_ys, quant_labels)
```

The age slope is $\hat\beta_1 =$ `r round(coef(quant_add)["age"], 2)` mg/dL per year for **every** BMI.

## Interaction: a twisted surface {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| dpi: 96
surface_plot(fram_pts, "age", "BMI", "totChol",
             surface_z(quant_int, quant_xs, quant_ys, "age", "BMI"),
             quant_xs, quant_ys, quant_labels)
```


## The slope is now a function {.smaller}

```{r}
quant_int |> tidy() |> kable(digits = 3)
```

$$
\text{slope of age} = \hat\beta_1 + \hat\beta_3 \times \text{BMI}
$$

```{r}
#| echo: false
b_q <- coef(quant_int)
tibble(BMI = c(21, 25, 31)) |>
  mutate(`Slope of age` = b_q["age"] + b_q["age:BMI"] * BMI) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

. . .

For a fixed BMI, the slope of age is a number. As BMI changes, the slope changes **linearly**: that is what a product term does.

::: question
Interpret $\hat\beta_3$: how does the age slope change for each one-unit increase in BMI?
:::

# The three cases

## Same idea, three pictures {.smaller}

| | Two categorical | One of each | Two quantitative |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Example | `diabetes_status` x `sex` | `age` x `sex` | `age` x `BMI` |
| Picture | jitter plot with group means | scatterplot with fitted lines | 3D surface |
| Additive model | same gap between groups at every level (parallel profiles) | parallel lines | flat tilted plane |
| Interaction adds | the 4th corner (a twist) | a different slope per group | a slope that changes with $X_2$ |
| $\hat\beta_3$ means | difference in differences | the **change in slope** from the reference group | change in the slope of $X_1$ per unit of $X_2$ |

. . .

In all three cases, the interaction term is $X_1 \times X_2$, and it is what **bends** the surface.

## Interactions and "holding constant" {.smaller}

Last time: a coefficient is the change in the mean response per unit change in that predictor, **holding the other predictors constant**.

. . .

With an interaction, that sentence is incomplete:

- There is **no single** effect of diabetes. There is one for women and one for men.
- Always describe the effect **at a particular value** of the other variable.

. . .

::: question
A patient asks, "How much does diabetes raise my blood pressure?" What should you say back?
:::

## Recap {.smaller}

- An **interaction** means the effect of one variable depends on the value of another.
- Categorical x categorical: the interaction terms are "differences in differences".
- Categorical x quantitative: each group gets its own slope (parallel lines become non-parallel).
- Quantitative x quantitative: the slope of one variable changes **linearly** with the other.
- Geometrically, an additive model is a **flat plane** and an interaction **twists** it.
- With an interaction, main effects are the effects at the reference level, not overall effects.
- An additive model can hide a big pattern. Plot the data first.
